Amazon:
- Raised 2026 capex to $220B vs. prior $200B (partly due to higher memory costs, which is bullish on $MU to Samsung) 
- Even at $220B, Amazon will not have enough capacity to meet all 2026 demand; Jassy expects the same in 2027.

Mostly read through on upstream semis. $GOOGL, $META, $AMZN, and $MSFT all identified compute shortage. 

All the narratives a few weeks earlier was "excess compute" from Meta and others + hyperscalers cutting back on spend... All BS. 

Amazon earnings was very bullish on AI semi trade. 

AXTI:

- AXT to double InP capacity during 2026. Then double again in 2027. 

This is expected to make AXT "by far the largest indium phosphide producer in the world." - LFG

- Q2 rev was $47.6M, the highest quarterly revenue in AXT history (InP revenue reached a record $30.7M, from DC applications.)
- Revenue increased 77% sequentially and 164% year over year.
- InP revenue-capacity targets: $60M per quarter exiting 2026.
- $130M per quarter exiting 2027 

That $130m target could be hiked too since management stated they find "whatever ways to increase that capacity expansion"

- Management said the reported backlog remains well above $100M, but that number no longer reflects all available demand.

"Customer demand continues to outpace supply, no matter how fast we add capacity." 800G/1.6T is driving the current cycle, while NPO/CPO extends it beyond 2027. 

Also they're targeting 50%-plus gross margin: "We should definitely be targeting a number that begins with a five."

China demand more than doubled, and their agreements with Casela, $COHR and $LITE did not materially drive Q2. 

This is not even considering my projected massive ASP hikes yet as InP substrates get more bottlenecked. 

TLDR:

- Amazon too much compute demands, needs capex to fufill it, so upstream semis go brrr. 
- AXT world largest InP substrate supplier, high gross margins, expansion, and supply can't keep up with demand.  

Bullish on demand side from Amazon + capex. Bullish on upstream optical supply chains from too much demand.

Seeing a lot of callbacks to Zach's post about iPhones vs hardware wallets.

I want to make something clear: Zach's point about UX is valid but if you can reason about a hardware wallet, IT IS STILL THE BEST OPTION.

The cold card attack was due to bad entropy in their seed-generation path. Many wallets have very very good entropy. Ledger specifically is tested/certified against AIS-31.

iPhones have good entropy too! But software-wallet key generation adds a trust requirement in the app, dependencies, OS/runtime, and device state. A bug in any of those can turn into compromised wallets. It also means handling signing keys inside a general-purpose, (potentially) internet-connected device.

A hardware wallet’s main advantage is that it isolates key generation and signing in a dedicated device, while letting you verify important transaction details on a trusted display. That materially reduces the attack surface.

Hardware wallets aren’t perfect. Neither are software wallets. But for users who can manage the UX safely, dedicated hardware remains the best option.

Basically the r/r for holding STRC at $100 is atrocious if we know they will always hit the ATM at $100, because you get all the downside volatility and only 1% yield every month as upside. Given the type of volatility STRC has (10% swings), if you short it at $100, you're almost certain that you'll get out in profit on its next drawdown.

Strategy claims that they target a 1% range at $99-$100, but that's physically impossible, because even if the dividend rate is variable in theory, in the short-term the div rate is fixed, meaning it will have a similar volatility profile as STRF, ie at least 10% swings.
If you cap the upside at $100, the 10% swings will be capped at $100 and you mechanically decrease the bottom of these volatile moves. I think it's much more realistic to target a $95-$105 range, because the average price of STRC would then be around $100 (which is the goal). In the current situation, by trying to be cute and "guarantee that STRC won't top $100", Strategy forces the whole thing to trade in a $90-$100 range (at best), meaning the average price of STRC is significantly below $100.

We shall create every missing piece of data to feed the models. The models just want to learn with their big computers. 

What I foresee is gigantic biological data factories: millions of standard lab machines, operated 24/7 by autonomous humanoid robots, with agents designing the next experiments in real time.

Every variable is captured: temperature, protocol, machine, reagent, timing, outcome, failure. Petabytes of clean, structured, verifiable data continuously flowing back into the models.

I call it bounded serendipity: creating a controlled space where AI can explore millions of experiments, encounter the unexpected, verify what works, and turn the physical world into both training data and scientific discovery.
